title: Morgan Stanley caps private credit fund withdrawals again as 11% seek exits
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Morgan Stanley is limiting withdrawals from its nearly $7 billion private credit fund for a third consecutive quarter after investors sought to redeem more than twice the amount available, according to Reuters.
The North Haven Private Income Fund capped third-quarter withdrawals at 5% of shares after investors submitted redemption requests covering 11.4%, according to a shareholder letter released Friday. The level was largely unchanged from the previous quarter.
Completed repurchases across three periods through September will total about $479 million, the fund said. Nearly two-thirds of the latest requests came from investors whose earlier attempts to withdraw money had already been limited during the previous two repurchase periods.
The continued restrictions come as private credit managers contend with investors seeking to pull money from the roughly $1.8 trillion market.
Redemption requests across major funds have eased in the latest quarter but remain elevated. Morgan Stanley joins other large asset managers, including Blackstone and BlackRock, that have continued restricting withdrawals from some private credit vehicles.
Fund managers are still dealing with a backlog of about $15 billion in redemption requests following record demand for withdrawals over the past year.
Investor concerns have included private credit underwriting standards and lenders’ exposure to older software investments, according to the report.
Private credit funds often offer investors periodic opportunities to redeem shares, subject to limits designed to avoid forced asset sales when withdrawal requests rise sharply. The structure means investors may receive only part of the amount requested when redemption demand exceeds a fund’s stated limit.
A separate Morgan Stanley fund with less than $1 billion in total investments also restricted withdrawals after investors requested redemptions representing about 7% of its shares.
The latest figures show withdrawal pressure remains present across parts of the private credit market despite the broader decline in redemption requests during the quarter.

title: Bitcoin jumps above $81k as short squeeze offsets rate and regulatory pressure
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Bitcoin surged above $81,000 on Saturday as a wave of short liquidations and renewed spot demand helped the cryptocurrency rebound from losses triggered by higher interest rates and a setback for U.S. crypto legislation.
Bitcoin climbed as high as $81,702 on Sept. 18 after trading near $76,400 a day earlier, marking its first move above $80,000 since Sept. 7. The world’s leading crypto was trading at $81,309.4 as of 22:50 ET (02:50 GMT) and was up 5.62% for the day.
The rebound followed a difficult week for risk assets. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis points, and the Bank of Japan followed with a quarter-point increase to 1.25%, its highest policy rate in 31 years.
Bitcoin initially fell toward $75,000-$76,000, but the expected selloff following the BOJ decision failed to materialize. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $159 million of inflows on Sept. 17, providing fresh spot demand.
A sharp short squeeze then accelerated Friday’s rally. Roughly $192 million of leveraged crypto positions were liquidated within one hour, including more than $183 million in shorts. Bitcoin shorts accounted for about $119 million of the total.
Regulatory uncertainty remains in focus after the U.S. Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act this week. The CFTC has since submitted a separate crypto market proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget, though details have not been disclosed.
The SEC has also introduced an innovation exemption providing qualifying platforms with a five-year route to offer onchain trading in certain tokenized stocks without registering as securities exchanges.
The CFTC separately issued relief allowing some software providers to connect users to regulated derivatives markets without registering as introducing brokers, subject to restrictions.
Market positioning points to cautious optimism after Bitcoin’s rebound. Myriad traders assigned an 84% probability to Bitcoin reaching $84,000 before falling to $55,000.
Confidence drops at higher levels. Polymarket traders put the probability of Bitcoin reaching $90,000 this year at 59%, but only 25% for $100,000. Downside risks also remain, with the platform assigning a 48% probability to Bitcoin touching $70,000 before year-end.

title: ProEnergy eyes $40 billion to $50 billion valuation in US IPO - Bloomberg
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- ProEnergy, a power-generation company backed by Energy Capital Partners, is seeking a valuation of as much as $50 billion in a potential U.S. initial public offering, Bloomberg reported exclusively, citing people familiar with the matter.
The company is working with Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase on preparations for the potential listing, according to the report. Depending on market conditions, an IPO could value ProEnergy at between $40 billion and $50 billion.
Energy Capital Partners could also consider selling the company instead of pursuing a listing, one person told Bloomberg. Discussions remain ongoing; the terms could change, and more banks could join the IPO process.
ECP paid about $275 million for a roughly 60% stake in ProEnergy in 2024, according to the report. Representatives for ECP, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan declined to comment, and ProEnergy did not immediately respond.
ProEnergy builds and tests gas turbines and develops smaller dispatchable power facilities. Its PE6000 aeroderivative gas turbine can generate enough electricity to power about 40,000 homes.
The company is seeking to capitalize on rising electricity demand from data centers as artificial intelligence infrastructure expands. In April, ProEnergy announced an agreement with AI infrastructure provider Crusoe covering 13 PE6000 turbines to supply power for data center projects.
ProEnergy is also positioning its natural gas-powered equipment as a source of electricity as coal plants are retired and new renewable generation remains under development.
A potential listing would follow several IPOs by companies tied to the expansion of AI data centers and their growing power requirements.
Investor reception after some of those listings has been mixed. Five of the 10 largest U.S. IPOs this year involve companies benefiting from AI data center construction, but several have struggled since going public.
Innio and Madison Air Solutions have each fallen at least 11% from IPO prices after raising more than $2.5 billion apiece.

title: Anthropic weighs new AI model launch as OpenAI gains ground - Reuters
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Anthropic is considering releasing a new artificial intelligence model as it faces growing competition from OpenAI ahead of an expected IPO, Reuters reported exclusively, citing three sources familiar with the matter.
The potential launch comes after OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, with the model gaining traction among businesses and developers. Some prospective Anthropic investors are reassessing the company’s position in enterprise AI as a result.
Anthropic is evaluating the safety of its next model as part of deliberations over a release, according to one source. The discussions come days after Chief Executive Dario Amodei called for the AI industry to slow the release of increasingly capable models over safety concerns.
The company is also weighing spending on new models against efforts to improve profitability as higher interest rates increase investor focus on when AI developers could generate sustainable cash flows.
Recent usage data points to increased competition. GPT-6 Astra represented about 13% of enterprise AI spending tracked by corporate expense platform Ramp, compared with roughly 8% for Anthropic’s Claude Fable.
OpenRouter also said users spent more on OpenAI models than Anthropic models last week, marking OpenAI’s first lead by that measure in more than two and a half years.
Anthropic still holds a revenue advantage. Its annualized revenue run rate exceeded $65 billion by the end of July, up from about $9 billion at the end of 2025. OpenAI’s annualized revenue run rate passed $40 billion in July.
Anthropic projects revenue of roughly $190 billion to $200 billion in 2028.
Investors cited by Reuters said open-source and open-weight models may pose a broader challenge by allowing businesses to lower costs and operate more AI infrastructure internally.
Meta Platforms, one of Anthropic’s largest customers, is seeking to reduce its reliance on Anthropic models as it develops more capabilities internally, according to the report.
Anthropic could push its IPO until after the November U.S. midterm elections. Earlier plans had called for IPO marketing to begin in mid-October at the earliest.

title: OpenAI expects $278 billion cash burn through 2030 - FT
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- OpenAI expects to burn through $278 billion in free cash flow between 2026 and the end of 2030 as spending on computing infrastructure surges, the Financial Times reported exclusively, citing a company presentation.
The projections were contained in a private presentation prepared in July in connection with a computing deal, according to the report.
OpenAI expects revenue to rise sharply over the same period, reaching $350 billion in 2030 from a projected $36 billion this year. Spending is nonetheless expected to outpace those gains as the ChatGPT maker commits heavily to the computing capacity needed to develop and operate its artificial intelligence models.
The scale of the projected cash burn highlights the capital requirements facing OpenAI as it expands infrastructure and competes with other major AI developers for computing resources.
OpenAI declined to comment on the financial projections.
The company has also been holding early discussions with investors about another fundraising round that could value it at more than $1.2 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering.
Chief Executive Sam Altman has said the company’s long-anticipated IPO remains planned but will not take place this year.
Raising additional private capital could give OpenAI more flexibility over the timing of a public listing. A new funding round could allow the company to delay an IPO by another one or two quarters.
Additional financing could also provide capital for mergers and acquisitions as OpenAI expands its operations and technology portfolio.
The discussions come as rapidly rising AI infrastructure requirements have pushed leading developers to secure large amounts of capital and computing capacity. OpenAI’s projections indicate that strong revenue growth alone is not expected to offset its planned spending over the next several years.
The company has not disclosed whether it intends to proceed with the potential fundraising round or when an IPO could eventually take place.

title: Oracle data center debt comes under pressure amid project concerns - FT
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- About $18 billion of loans tied to an Oracle-leased data center in New Mexico have come under pressure, with banks quoting the debt at 89 to 91 cents on the dollar, the Financial Times reported exclusively.
The loans are linked to Project Jupiter, a 1,400-acre data center campus in Doña Ana County that forms part of Oracle’s broader agreement with OpenAI to supply artificial intelligence computing capacity.
A consortium of banks provided about $18 billion in loans late last year to fund construction of the project. Syndicate banks involved include Santander and Jefferies.
Attempts to distribute the debt to a wider group of investors have stalled amid concerns about Oracle’s increasing borrowing and weaker credit profile, according to the report. That has left banks holding more Oracle-linked project debt on their balance sheets than initially planned.
Oracle’s corporate credit rating is one notch above junk after S&P downgraded the company in July.
The pressure comes as Oracle increases spending on AI infrastructure, adding to investor scrutiny of its debt load. The company has committed substantial capital to expanding the computing capacity needed to serve growing demand for artificial intelligence services.
Project Jupiter is also facing local opposition over concerns about its potential impact on water supplies and air quality, raising questions over the development of the site.
The campus was initially expected to receive power from 2.2 gigawatts of gas turbines. New Mexico’s state land office has since blocked a request to run a natural gas pipeline to the data center, according to the report.
The combination of financing pressure and uncertainty surrounding the project’s power infrastructure could complicate efforts to complete the campus as planned.
Oracle, Santander and Jefferies did not respond to requests for comment.

title: US fashion council CEO Kolb resigns after clash with runway show protesters
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
By Ruchika Khanna
Sept 18 (Reuters) - Steven Kolb resigned as head of the Council of Fashion Designers of America on Friday, days after coming under fire for physically restraining animal rights activists at a New York Fashion Week runway show.
"After twenty years leading the CFDA, I have made the difficult decision to step down as CEO and President," Kolb said in a post on his Substack.
The CFDA, the leading US fashion-industry trade group and organizer of New York Fashion Week, said on Tuesday that Kolb was on leave pending a full review by the council’s board, after he said he was taking a voluntary leave.
On Sunday, Kolb grabbed at least two activists protesting H&M-owned COS’s use of wool during a runway show. He pinned one protester to the ground and covered her mouth with his hand, according to videos viewed by Reuters that circulated widely online.
Kolb apologized on Monday, saying he planned to meet with People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, which had organized the protest.
"There is no justification for physically restraining another person," he said at the time. "Security should have handled the situation, and I should have stepped back."
Kolb’s physical confrontation with the activists led to a widespread backlash, with PETA on Sunday saying his actions "show how top people in fashion use violence to silence people" advocating for animal rights.
The CFDA board, led by Thom Browne and including designers such as Vera Wang, Ralph Lauren and Michael Kors, said in an Instagram post that it respected Kolb’s decision to step down and thanked him for his years of service.
The CFDA did not name a successor.

title: U.S. approves potential $2.7 billion air defense sale to Ukraine
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- The U.S. State Department has approved a potential $2.7 billion military sale to Ukraine covering air defense upgrades, weapons, and related equipment and services, according to a congressional notification late Friday.
The proposed package includes S-300 clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, range-extended laser-guided rockets, launcher and mobile launching system modification kits, and counter-drone radars, the State Department said.
The sale remains subject to congressional review and has not yet been finalized.
If completed, Ukraine would finance the purchase through a combination of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing funds appropriated during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Foreign Military Financing provides grants that allow foreign governments to purchase U.S.-made weapons and defense equipment.
The State Department said the U.S. financing would be counted as a capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund through a one-for-one reimbursement arrangement.
The fund was established as part of a minerals agreement signed between Washington and Kyiv last year.
The proposed sale comes as the Trump administration seeks to shift more of the financial burden for supporting Ukraine toward European countries.
President Donald Trump earlier this month said he would ask European nations to reimburse the United States for military aid and munitions previously supplied to Ukraine.
The potential weapons package also follows Trump’s signing on Friday of legislation aimed at increasing economic pressure on Russia.
Trump had pledged to bring the Russia-Ukraine conflict to an end after taking office early last year, but fighting has continued 20 months into his presidency. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
The financing arrangement for the proposed $2.7 billion sale would combine European contributions with previously appropriated U.S. military assistance if the transaction clears congressional review and is completed.

title: How to position for the next wave of AI-led scientific breakthroughs
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Artificial intelligence is moving beyond text generation into scientific research, creating investment opportunities across AI infrastructure, pharmaceuticals, nuclear fusion, industrial materials and utilities, according to UBS Wealth Management.
The shift was highlighted by OpenAI’s recent mathematical proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, a centuries-old fluid dynamics problem and one of seven Millennium Prize Problems.
OpenAI used 10,000 autonomous AI agents working in parallel for 88 hours. The system identified a scenario in which fluid forces accelerate infinitely, causing a mathematical breakdown, before formalizing the proof using Lean, a system for machine-checked mathematical validation.
The development could have implications for fields ranging from aviation aerodynamics to nuclear fusion. Three areas stand out for their commercial potential: drug development, fusion energy and advanced materials.
In pharmaceuticals, multi-agent AI systems can simulate millions of protein variations in the cloud, testing characteristics such as toxicity, stability in the bloodstream and manufacturing resilience before physical laboratory work begins. More than 170 AI-designed programs are already in development or clinical evaluation, including Phase III trials.
AI could also play a critical role in nuclear fusion by helping stabilize highly turbulent plasma. Reinforcement-learning systems can analyze reactor data, predict plasma disruptions around 200 milliseconds before they occur, and adjust magnetic coils thousands of times per second.
Commercial fusion could benefit electricity-intensive AI infrastructure alongside manufacturing, utilities, and grid infrastructure.
Materials science represents another opportunity. AI models can test millions of elemental combinations daily in search of properties needed for lighter, higher-density batteries, lower-heat computing hardware and potential room-temperature superconductors.
The broader investment case centers on AI becoming a tool for automating scientific research rather than simply generating content. Companies exposed to AI infrastructure, pharmaceuticals, industrial materials and utilities could benefit as these technologies move from research toward commercial applications.

title: Saudi alerts sound as Yemen fighting puts key oil shipping routes under pressure
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Saudi Arabia issued repeated danger alerts for Riyadh and al-Kharj overnight as fighting with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis intensified, raising fresh concerns over two major Middle East shipping routes already disrupted by the Iran war.
Saudi Civil Defence later said the danger had passed. The warnings came amid an expanding Houthi missile and drone campaign that has targeted Saudi cities, military bases and energy infrastructure.
The Houthis said Saudi Arabia carried out 26 strikes on areas under their control over the previous 24 hours and about 300 during the past week. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government separately said its forces killed 30 Houthi fighters and wounded more than 60 in clashes in Taiz province.
Shipping risks have grown after Houthi territorial gains around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Commercial vessels are still using the waterway, but traffic fell to around 26 to 35 vessels a day this week from an average of 35 to 40 over the previous eight weeks, according to Kpler data cited by CBS.
Only five laden vessels carrying Saudi products exited the Red Sea through Bab el-Mandeb over the past seven days.
The pressure comes as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted. Two vessels were attacked there on Friday, according to a U.K. naval agency, and Iran claimed responsibility for striking one ship it said was attempting an "illegal crossing."
U.S. Central Command said its blockade has redirected 105 commercial vessels travelling to or from Iranian ports. More than 30 million barrels of Iranian or likely Iranian crude have been kept inside the Persian Gulf.
Brent crude was around $104 a barrel on Friday, compared with $88 three weeks earlier. France said it plans to convene a G7 energy meeting that could discuss releasing strategic reserves.
President Donald Trump also signed legislation extending existing U.S. sanctions authorities against Iran for another five years, through 2031.
The financial cost of the conflict is climbing. U.S. Central Command estimated American military spending on the war at $43.6 billion through Sept. 3, including $28.1 billion for munitions. Pentagon figures cited by the Chicago Tribune showed 18 U.S. troops killed and more than 830 wounded.

title: UBS now expects AI capex to reach nearly $1tn this year and around $1.4tn by 2027
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- UBS now expects artificial intelligence capital expenditure to reach nearly $1 trillion in 2026 before climbing to around $1.4 trillion in 2027, with surging memory costs accounting for most of the increase.
The bank’s updated estimates put total AI capex at $998 billion this year, almost double the $506 billion recorded in 2025. Spending is forecast to rise again to $1.447 trillion next year.
Memory is emerging as the main source of that growth as prices rise sharply.
UBS estimates memory spending will climb from $71 billion in 2025 to $367 billion this year and $923 billion in 2027. Other AI-related costs are estimated at $631 billion in 2026 before declining to $525 billion next year.
That means higher memory costs will account for about 60% of the increase in AI capex this year and more than the entire net increase in 2027, as spending on other components falls.
Across the two years, UBS calculates that roughly 90% of the nearly $1 trillion increase in AI capital expenditure between 2025 and 2027 will come from higher memory spending.
The shift would also dramatically change the composition of AI investment. Memory represented about 14% of total AI capex in 2025, according to the bank. Its share is estimated to rise to 37% this year and reach 64% in 2027.
The increase carries broader economic implications depending on whether the additional spending reflects higher memory prices or greater volumes.
UBS said price-driven increases would add relatively little to real U.S. gross domestic product. Instead, the spending would represent a transfer of income and profits toward memory producers in Asia, providing a positive contribution to GDP in those economies.
The estimates highlight how the economics of the AI investment cycle are shifting from the scale of infrastructure spending alone toward the rising cost of the components needed to support increasingly powerful computing systems.

title: Google Gemini hacked three companies during cybersecurity test - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Google’s Gemini AI breached systems belonging to three companies during a cybersecurity test, the first known case of the company’s AI autonomously carrying out such intrusions, the Wall Street Journal reported exclusively.
The incidents occurred in May during cybersecurity evaluations conducted by AI security testing company Irregular. Google confirmed the breaches on Friday after the Journal contacted the company with questions.
In one case, Gemini guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In two other test runs, the model found credentials in publicly accessible online repositories and successfully used them to enter systems belonging to real companies.
Google said Gemini stopped each intrusion after recognizing that it had accessed a real company’s systems rather than the fictional target used in the test. The company said no harm occurred and that it notified all three affected businesses.
The incidents stemmed from a capture-the-flag exercise designed to test Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities. The model was supposed to retrieve information from a fictional company operating inside Irregular’s testing infrastructure.
The fictional business shared its name with a real company, and the testing environment unintentionally gave Gemini internet access. As a result, the model targeted real-world systems while trying to complete the exercise.
Irregular notified Google about the incidents in late July. Google did not publicly disclose them at the time and said it does not consider the behavior an example of AI model misalignment, pointing to Gemini’s decision to stop after recognizing the unintended breaches.
Google also notified U.S. federal authorities but declined to identify the companies involved or specify which Gemini model carried out the intrusions. It said the incidents did not involve its newest model.
The episode adds to scrutiny over the cybersecurity capabilities of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Similar testing incidents involving models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta have previously resulted in systems reaching targets outside their intended testing environments.

title: California judge blocks part of TikTok’s $400 million privacy settlement
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- A California federal judge tentatively rejected part of the U.S. government’s $400 million settlement with TikTok over alleged children’s privacy violations, potentially keeping additional oversight of the social media platform in place, Bloomberg reported.
U.S. District Judge George H. Wu on Friday tentatively denied a request to vacate an order originally imposed on Musical.ly, the predecessor to TikTok that was acquired by Beijing-based ByteDance.
The order covers privacy protections for users under the age of 13. Wu said neither TikTok nor the U.S. government had shown that the obligations imposed under the earlier order were no longer needed.
The ruling could affect part of TikTok’s $400 million settlement reached with the U.S. government in August to resolve child privacy allegations initially raised under the Biden administration.
Of that amount, $100 million was contingent on the earlier consent decree being vacated.
Wu said changes to TikTok’s ownership structure, its compliance measures and the latest settlement did not establish that the company had substantially complied with the existing order or that its protections were no longer necessary.
The judge indicated that he intends to retain oversight of TikTok’s privacy practices.
The decision adds another complication to TikTok’s U.S. operations after years of government scrutiny tied to the platform’s Chinese ownership.
A deal finalized between the Trump administration and ByteDance in January transferred parts of TikTok’s U.S. operations to American investors, appearing to resolve a separate dispute over the platform’s ownership and operations in the country.
The subsequent $400 million privacy settlement in August addressed allegations involving protections for younger users.
TikTok and the U.S. Department of Justice did not respond to Bloomberg’s requests for comment after business hours.
Wu’s decision remains tentative, with a hearing on the government’s request to dismiss the consent decree scheduled for Sept. 21.

title: Barclays says AI trade is maturing, favors greater diversification
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Barclays told clients in a note on Friday that it believes the artificial intelligence trade is entering a more mature phase, calling for greater diversification even as it welcomed clarity from the Federal Reserve.
Strategist Emmanuel Cau said the Fed's 25-basis-point hike was arguably the least bad outcome for markets, reinforcing its credibility and commitment to lowering inflation.
He feels the meeting should "ultimately be seen as a clearing event and a positive development," noting the dollar has stabilized, long-end yields eased and equities rose after the decision.
Still, Cau notes that the global monetary backdrop continues to tighten, implying lower valuations and potentially lower equity returns. He added that it was hard to see rates and equities fully stabilizing until energy-related inflation pressures ease.
On AI, Cau said the theme has evolved from a one-way trade into a more volatile one, with growing dispersion between winners and losers as investors question the sustainability of hyperscaler capital spending.
Recent calls from Anthropic and other developers for a slower pace of AI development have added to those doubts.
While Barclays still views AI as a tailwind for growth and earnings, Cau said "the trade is clearly entering a more mature phase with both volatility and execution risks rising."
That argues for greater diversification and a broadening of market leadership into less AI-exposed areas, particularly outside U.S. technology, he said, noting the valuation gap between the U.S. and the rest of the world has begun to narrow.

title: Survey shows Apple is seeing a better-than-expected iPhone refresh cycle
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Evercore ISI told investors in a note that its latest consumer survey points to a stronger-than-expected iPhone upgrade cycle for Apple, with pricing set to provide a sizable tailwind.
The firm's annual survey of nearly 4,000 consumers is said to have pointed to a "better-than-expected iPhone refresh cycle," led by the newest models.
Beyond unit strength, Evercore said pricing could rise more than 20%, driven by higher list prices, pricier models and a shift toward larger memory configurations.
"Pro Max Remains King," the firm wrote, with 53% of respondents planning to buy the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, and 32% specifically eyeing the Pro Max, up from 29% a year ago.
Demand for the new foldable iPhone Duo looked more subdued at 14%, though Evercore expects that to improve closer to its mid-October launch.
The survey showed upgrades increasingly driven by aging devices, with 67% of respondents citing an old iPhone, up from 48% last year.
As consumers gravitate toward higher memory tiers and Apple rolls out 2-terabyte Pro and Duo models, the firm sees average selling prices rising about 28%.
Evercore also flagged stronger interest in wearables, with Apple Watch purchase intentions at 38% and AirPods at 43%, both up on last year.
It cautioned the survey is U.S.-specific, but said demand appears modestly ahead of last year and points to upside to fiscal 2027 revenue versus Street estimates of about 7% growth. The firm kept its outperform rating and raised its target to $380.

title: China opens probes into four online travel booking platforms
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
Investing.com -- Chinese regulators have opened investigations into four online hotel and travel booking platforms over suspected practices that may hurt competition and merchant rights, Bloomberg reported on Saturday.
The investigations target Hangzhou Taomei Aviation Service, Tongcheng Network Technology, Tujia Online Information Technology (Tianjin) and Beijing Sankuai Information Technology, according to a statement from the Beijing Municipal Administration for Market Regulation.
The probes follow a broader regulatory review of China’s online travel sector and a meeting with hotel and travel booking platforms convened by the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
Authorities are examining business practices that may affect fair competition and the rights of merchants using the platforms.
The China Hospitality Association backed the investigations and called on booking platforms to provide greater transparency around their trading rules and algorithms.
The industry group specifically cited search rankings, traffic allocation, commission rates and promotional programs as areas where platforms should provide clearer information to merchants.
It also called for greater industry self-discipline and closer cooperation between online booking platforms and hospitality businesses.
The latest action extends regulatory scrutiny of China’s online hotel and travel booking industry after authorities imposed a 5.18 billion yuan ($765 million) antitrust penalty on Trip.com Group in July.
Trip.com was fined for abusing its dominant position in China’s online hotel booking market.
The investigations signal continued regulatory attention on how major online travel platforms interact with hotels and other merchants, particularly in areas such as commissions, platform traffic, and promotional practices.
No penalties or findings against the four platforms named in the latest investigations were announced.

title: Trump says his son told him he will repay Russian oligarch for wedding parties
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
By Jacob Bogage and Steve Holland
WASHINGTON, Sept 18 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Friday his son, Donald Trump Jr., has told him he would pay back a Russian oligarch who bankrolled wedding celebrations for him in the Bahamas in May.
Democrats in the US Congress launched an investigation this week into reports that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding festivities.
ProPublica, which first reported Kremlev’s involvement, said he has close ties to the Russian government.
Trump told reporters on Friday that when he asked his son about the report, he responded, "’No, I’m paying it back, Dad.’ And that was a while ago. So I heard he’s paying."
A person familiar with the situation confirmed that Don Jr. planned to reimburse Kremlev.
Kremlev and the IBA did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Friday.
The president, who did not attend his son’s wedding, said in a statement earlier in the week that he does not know Kremlev and that the wedding controversy is "not a big deal!"
Trump said on Friday he has given wedding parties to "numerous people" at "beautiful places" like his Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida.
"They get married, I give them a party," Trump said. "With all of that being said, I understand that Don’s paid him back."
Don Jr.’s wife, Bettina Trump, in an Instagram post on Monday called Kremlev a friend who extended an "extraordinarily generous wedding gift," stressing that Kremlev paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.

title: AfD surge in eastern Germany makes some immigrants question whether they still belong
full_text:
U.S. stocks end mixed for the week as traders digest Fed hike, AI safety uproar
By Amina Ismail and James Mackenzie
ROSTOCK, Germany, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Shahd Najeeb still remembers the trauma of fleeing Islamic State fighters during Syria’s civil war. More than a decade after finding refuge in Germany, she now fears she may no longer be welcome there.
"When I think about the time we left Syria, I still don’t know how we managed to get through it," she told Reuters in her home in Rostock, on Germany’s Baltic coast. "It was like a nightmare."
Najeeb and her husband, Mahmoud Hmouech, fled their home in Deir al-Zor in eastern Syria and rebuilt their lives in Germany, where he works in a barber shop and she serves meals in local schools. They have two young children.
"We are grateful to the German people for welcoming us and giving us peace and security," Hmouech said. "The work we do is a small way of showing our gratitude."
They are among more than 900,000 Syrians living in Germany, most of whom arrived as asylum seekers during the civil war.
But as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) gains support and migration returns to the centre of political debate, migrants say hostility towards foreigners is growing.
Reuters spoke to 20 people of migrant background in Rostock and the nearby city of Schwerin, many of whom have become German citizens and have lived in Germany for years.
Most said they had encountered more anti-immigrant abuse in recent years, ranging from muttered remarks to demands that they return to their countries of origin. One woman said a neighbour poured foul-smelling water on her from a balcony.
Their concerns come as the AfD gains momentum across eastern Germany.
In Najeeb and Hmouech’s home state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, in the formerly communist east, opinion polls suggest the AfD is set to become the biggest party in an election on Sunday.
Earlier this month, the party, which wants to restrict immigration and talks about "remigration" - or sending foreigners back to their home countries - won its first major regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, another eastern state.
Several interviewees, including people working in healthcare, tourism, education and food services, said they would consider leaving Rostock or Schwerin if the climate continued to worsen.
’THIS COUNTRY IS FOR GERMANS’
Sitting in the family’s small apartment in northern Rostock, where their children’s drawings cover one wall and toys are neatly stacked in corners of the living room, Najeeb spoke as her children, aged 6 and 4, played nearby.
Najeeb, who studied physics in Baghdad and later worked as a jewellery designer in Syria, recalled stopping at a grocery store after collecting her children from school when, she said, an elderly man in a wheelchair shouted that she did not belong in Germany.
"This country is for Germans," he yelled.
"The pain I experienced in Rostock is a new kind of pain that I have never felt before," Najeeb said.
"You feel the injustice because you have done nothing wrong. I worked hard to build a life for myself and then someone comes along and treats you like garbage," she said, her voice cracking.
She recalled her son asking: "Mama, why is he insulting you? What did you do to him?" Unsure how to explain, she told him the man was perhaps unwell.
LABOUR FORCE
The AfD began as a eurosceptic party in 2013 and its anti-immigrant tone sharpened markedly after former Chancellor Angela Merkel’s decision in 2015 to open Germany’s borders temporarily, admitting around one million migrants and refugees, around a third of them Syrians fleeing the civil war.
Since then, it has grown from a fringe movement into Germany’s most popular party, leading Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservatives in national polls.
Leif-Erik Holm, the AfD’s main candidate in Sunday’s election, says he has "absolutely no objection" to immigration by skilled workers. He says those who should be deported are the more than 250,000 foreigners who have no legal right to stay in Germany.
But critics say the broader problem is the atmosphere created by rhetoric they say targets foreigners in general.
During a televised debate on Wednesday, Social Democrat state premier Manuela Schwesig accused the AfD of "causing widespread fear with its statements on remigration and workers from different cultural backgrounds."
"I think it’s terrible that people who work here, who make their contribution and pay their taxes and social security contributions, are afraid and don’t feel at ease," she said.
During the debate, she and Holm took a question from a design engineer concerned at the risk of losing a valued Moroccan draughtsman because of the racist insults he said he encountered regularly on the street.
Holm said it was "naturally a shame that there’s such a mood". But he blamed the government for allowing illegal immigration and failing to deport more than a fraction of foreigners formally required to leave the country.
The debate carries economic implications as well.
Around 50,000 people with a migration background work in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Economists have warned that like other eastern states with low birth rates and an ageing population, it will need more skilled workers.
According to data from Germany’s labour office, around 316,000 Syrian nationals - not including Syrians who have acquired German nationality - work in Germany, most in full-time jobs that pay social security contributions.
Their unemployment rate is above 30%, but data show the longer people stay, the more likely they are to find work. Figures from 2023 indicate that among those who have been in Germany for seven years or longer, more than 60% have a job.
Many Syrians say they hope to return home if conditions improve. Others, including Najeeb and Hmouech, increasingly see their future in Germany.
Whether the AfD’s rise changes that calculation remains an open question.
Hmouech says he does not want his children to grow up feeling rejected by the society they call home.
"At the end of the day, family comes first," he said.
